title: Rounding Number Line
context: Grade 4, near the end. An adult sees three rounding procedures. What the page is actually doing is asking for a judgement twice over: which multiple is nearer, and then whether swapping the number for it was a sensible thing to do at all.

writeup.why: Swap a number for a rounder one that is near enough, and work out when that is a bad idea.
writeup.look: A number line with your number marked on it and the two nearest round numbers waiting at either end.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Rounding Number Line' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number being rounded and, under it, the place it is being rounded to, both in ink, with the two candidate multiples beside them; on the third phase it holds the three answers in a column as they are made, and on the fourth it carries the quantity and what the quantity is for, because nothing in the judgement bay is counted. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. A place picker of three keys 200 by 64 runs along the top of the working area at 64,214, 284,214 and 504,214, reading nearest ten, nearest hundred and nearest thousand, the chosen one sitting proud of the other two; stack all three, 180 by 64, sits at 764,214 and snap, 180 by 64, at 970,214. The line itself is a ruled 880 at 156,400 with a tick 4 by 48 at each end and a label plate 180 by 56 centred under each end at 66,420 and 946,420, carrying the two candidate multiples. The halfway tick stands at the midpoint, 4 by 72, with a small diamond at its head and the halfway value printed above it. The marker is a drawn pin 36 by 76 standing on the line at the number's own place with the number printed on its head; it is the one thing on the stage that never moves while the line zooms, because the zoom is drawn as the ends coming in towards it. The two distance bars lie under the line at y 490, 20 tall, running from the foot of the marker out to each end with their lengths printed at their middles, and the shorter of the two fills amber the moment both are drawn. The rule strip is 700 by 96 at 156,530: the number printed across it in ruled place columns, the rounding place shaded amber, and one single box closed round the whole of what stands to its right, however many digits that is, with what that box holds printed under it as one number in words and the threshold, five or more, fifty or more, five hundred or more, printed beside it. The answer plate is 220 by 96 at 886,530. On the third phase the line is drawn three times, 660 long at 136,268, 136,402 and 136,536, each with its own end plates 140 by 48 and its own answer plate 200 by 56 at x 900, and the three markers stand very nearly one above another, because the number has not moved and only the zoom has. On the fourth phase the quantity card is 1086 by 140 at 64,214 and the two argument cards are 520 by 300 at 64,378 and 630,378, headed round it and keep it, each with room for a reason; that bay has no answer key, so neither card is ever marked and the marker never snaps there. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across on the first three phases, with a thirteenth key that writes a run of zeros so a rounded answer can be finished in one press; on the fourth it is a choice pad of two large keys, round it and keep it, with a strip of reason words under them, and nothing pressed on that pad is ever marked right or wrong. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the ones period is deep blue, the thousands period green, the lakhs period vermilion and the millions period rose; whatever settles the answer on this stage is amber; a zero that is only holding a place open is grey; and chrome never borrows one of them, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
writeup.finish: The card shows one number rounded all three ways on its line, and the judgement the child made about a number that should not be rounded.

phases.win: the marker lands on the nearer ten and the rule strip agrees
phases.does: reads the ones digit, compares the distances and snaps the marker
phases.goal: the ones digit alone decides rounding to the nearest ten
phases.says: Which end is your number closer to? Look before you count.
phases.check: Away from the screen: which two tens is your house number between, and which of them is it nearer to?
phases.feels: you can see which end is nearer before anybody has said a word about digits
phases.hands: Draw a line on paper, write the ten below the number at one end and the ten above it at the other, mark the middle, and let the child put a finger on the number and walk it to each end, counting the steps out loud both ways.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which two tens sit either side of it? Second rung, the phase's: which bar is shorter? Third rung: the line is zoomed until the two ends are a hand's width apart and the child points at the nearer end before writing anything down. The pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: the place being rounded to is the tens place, so the tens digit looks like the one to read.
wrong.move: reads the tens digit instead of the ones digit and rounds the number down.
wrong.screen: the rounding place shades amber on the rule strip and the box to its right closes round the ones digit alone, with what it holds printed under it; on the line the two distance bars fill outward from the foot of the marker and the shorter one fills amber. The child's answer stays in the slot beside them.

wrong.why: only the tens digit was said to change, so the rest of the number looks as though it should be left alone.
wrong.move: writes the rounded answer with the ones digit left exactly as it was.
wrong.screen: the child's answer is given its own marker and dropped onto the line: it lands somewhere between the two ends rather than on either of them, and the two end plates light as the only two places an answer can sit. The ones place then rolls down to a grey zero and that marker slides the rest of the way onto the end.

phases.screen: the line zoomed so that two neighbouring tens sit at its ends
phases.soWhat: Rounding to the nearest ten is taking the nearer of the two tens either side, and the ones digit is how you tell which.

phases.win: the whole two digit remainder is highlighted, not just one digit
phases.does: covers the hundreds digit, reads what is left and snaps
phases.goal: for hundreds you read the two digits to the right as one number
phases.says: Cover the hundreds. Read what is left as one number, not two.
phases.check: Cover the hundreds digit here. What number is left, and is it more than halfway to the next hundred?
phases.feels: two digits stop being two digits and turn into one number that is either side of halfway
phases.hands: Cover the hundreds digit with a thumb, read out loud what is left to the right of it as one number, and only then say which hundred the number is nearer to.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does the box to the right of the amber place hold? Second rung, the phase's: is that number past halfway? Third rung: the strip is cut to the last two digits with the halfway value labelled beside them, and the child says over or under. The pad stays open.

wrong.why: the nearest ten was settled by the single digit next door, so the nearest hundred looks as though it works the same way.
wrong.move: reads only the tens digit and rounds the number down.
wrong.screen: the box on the rule strip opens wider until it holds both digits to the right of the amber place, and what they make together is printed under it as one number in words with the threshold beside it; on the line the bars fill and the shorter one fills amber. The child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the rule for tens was one digit against five, so two digits look like that same rule done twice.
wrong.move: reads the two digits to the right as two separate numbers and measures each against five.
wrong.screen: the two digits slide together inside one box and are read out as a single number; the halfway tick on the line takes a label saying what it stands for, and the marker is shown standing past that tick or short of it, with nothing said about digits at all.

phases.screen: the line zoomed to two neighbouring hundreds
phases.soWhat: For hundreds I read everything to the right of the hundreds place as one number and measure it against halfway.

phases.win: the three answers stand together and none of them is crossed out
phases.does: rounds to the nearest thousand and compares all three answers
phases.goal: one number can round three different ways and all three are right
phases.says: Three answers from one number. Are any of them wrong?
phases.check: You rounded a number and got a different answer from your friend. What is the first thing to ask each other?
phases.feels: three answers out of one number, and being asked to cross one out and finding you cannot
phases.hands: Round one number to the nearest ten, hundred and thousand on three lines ruled under each other on one sheet, and write the three answers in a column so they can be read down together.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many digits stand to the right of the thousands place? Second rung, the phase's: what number do they make together, and is it past halfway? Third rung: only the thousands line is left on the stage with both ends labelled. The pad stays open and none of the earlier answers is taken away.

wrong.why: a number with something in it looks like a number to go up on, and going up is what the rule has mostly done so far.
wrong.move: rounds up to the next thousand because the hundreds place is not empty.
wrong.screen: the lowest line zooms until the two thousands sit at its ends and the marker is left standing near the left one; the box on the rule strip closes round all three digits to the right of the amber place and prints them as one number, with the halfway value printed at the halfway tick. The bars fill and the left one is plainly the shorter.

wrong.why: one number has had one answer every time until now, so three answers look like two mistakes and a success.
wrong.move: says two of the three answers must be wrong, because they do not agree.
wrong.screen: the three lines stack and a line drops from each marker to the one below it and stands very nearly upright, because the number is the same on all three and only the zoom is different, while the three answers stay where they landed; each answer then takes its own label, to the nearest ten, to the nearest hundred, to the nearest thousand, and not one of them is crossed out.

phases.screen: the same number rounded three ways, stacked
phases.soWhat: One number rounds three different ways, and an answer only means something once you say what it was rounded to.

phases.win: the reason is given and it is about the use, not about the digits
phases.does: decides whether the number should be rounded and gives a reason
phases.goal: whether to round depends on what the number is for
phases.says: Ask what this number is for before you round it.
phases.check: Name one number in this house that must never be rounded, and say what would go wrong if it were.
phases.feels: the rule works perfectly and you still should not use it
phases.hands: Take a bill or a timetable from the kitchen, read out three numbers on it, and ask of each one whether rounding it would matter, and to whom it would matter.
phases.tries: This bay has no answer key, so the ladder asks rather than narrows. First rung, from the item: who uses this number? Second rung, the phase's: what do they do with it? Third rung: the same quantity is put in two places, on a poster and on a ticket, and the child answers for each of them. Both argument cards stay open and neither is ever marked.

wrong.why: the number is there, the rule works on it perfectly, and nothing on the page says to stop.
wrong.move: rounds the school's starting time to the nearest ten minutes because the rule allows it.
wrong.screen: the bay does not snap and nothing is marked. The rounded time is printed on a card beside the true one and the morning is drawn along the foot of the bay in three small frames, the gate, the bell and a child arriving at the rounded time; both cards stay side by side and the argument card is left open.

wrong.why: the number is big enough to look like an estimate, and a rounder number is easier to hold on to.
wrong.move: rounds the count of bones in the body to the nearest hundred and reads the rounded figure back as the fact.
wrong.screen: the two figures are printed one under the other and a row of small bones is drawn beside each, counted along in tens, so the gap between the two counts is drawn rather than stated. The child's reason card stays open and neither figure is crossed out.

phases.screen: the judgement bay holding a real quantity and two arguments
phases.soWhat: Whether to round depends on what the number is for, and a number somebody has to act on is left alone.
phases.concept: When rounding a number would be wrong

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the third answer lands. The three lines fold together into one, at the widest of the three zooms, and the three markers slide into a single pin, because they were the same number all along. The three answers then come down onto that one line as three separate ticks, each keeping its own label: two of them in close beside the pin and the third right out at the end of the line. One pin, three ticks, and nothing to choose between them. Nothing else moves and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first two phases the line is already drawn across the working area, zoomed so that the two candidate multiples sit at its ends with their labels under them, the halfway tick standing between them, the marker for the number already on the line where the number belongs, and the two distance bars ruled but unfilled. On the third the line is drawn three times, one under another, and the top two carry the answers made on the earlier phases while the lowest stands empty. On the fourth there is no line at all: the judgement bay is up with its quantity printed on a card, a line under it saying who uses that number, and two argument cards face up and blank. The running count at the top left is empty and the slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the marker on the first three phases, or the quantity card on the fourth, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks which end is nearer. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number, any rounding place, with the judgement bay open alongside. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on rounding three ways and on judging when a number should be left alone.
voiceLines: Your number is on the line. Which end is it nearer?
Which end is your number closer to? Look before you count.
Cover the hundreds. Read what is left as one number, not two.
Three answers from one number. Are any of them wrong?
Ask what this number is for before you round it.
The same number. A different place to round it to.
Free play. Any number, any place, and the judgement bay open.
Look at the two ends again, and at the mark halfway between them.
You took the nearer one every time, and then asked whether to take it at all.

observations.why: The two candidates sit at the ends of the line and the marker sits where the number is.
observations.soWhat: Rounding is choosing the nearer of two round numbers, and the rule only describes that choice.
observations.observe: The marker was plainly nearer one end before a single digit had been read.

observations.why: Everything standing to the right of the rounding place is one number, however many digits it has.
observations.soWhat: I read the whole of what is to the right of the place, not the digit next door to it.
observations.observe: Rounding to the nearest hundred read two digits at once, and to the nearest thousand it read three.

observations.why: Each answer is the nearer multiple of a different size.
observations.soWhat: A rounded number means nothing until you say what it was rounded to.
observations.observe: One number gave three different answers and not one of them was crossed out.

observations.why: Whether to round depends on what the number is for, and the number cannot say that.
observations.soWhat: Some questions about a number are settled by its use and not by its digits.
observations.observe: The judgement bay took an answer and gave none back.

source_tool.description: A number line runs across the stage and the number being rounded sits on it as a marker. Choosing nearest ten, hundred or thousand zooms the line so that exactly the two candidate multiples sit at its ends, with the halfway point marked between them. The marker's distance to each end is drawn as a bar, so which one is nearer is seen before it is worked out, and the rounded answer then snaps to the nearer end. A rule strip beneath shows which digits were read to make the decision, highlighting the whole number to the right of the rounding place rather than a single digit. Rounding the same number all three ways stacks the three answers so they can be compared. A second bay drops the rounding rule and asks instead whether a given number ought to be rounded at all, taking a real quantity and letting the child argue both ways.
source_tool.art_direction: A number line between two round numbers / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.
Drawn things, not abstract boxes: token tiles, place value charts with ruled columns, a number line with labelled ticks, digit cards that can be picked up, and lettered tiles for the Roman numerals.

A large number is always shown with its digits sitting in named places, with the period bands behind them and the commas drawn where the Indian system puts them. A bare numeral with no chart behind it is never used to teach place value.
Where tokens or blocks stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A place is told apart by its column label first and by its band colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a token or a place the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The ones period is deep blue, the thousands period is green and the lakhs period is vermilion, and those three bands are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The millions period is rose and appears only where the international chart does. A digit under discussion, or the digit that decides a comparison, is amber. A zero holding an empty place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a period is told apart by its band and its label before its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the two ends again, and at the mark halfway between them.
voice.onNext: The same number. A different place to round it to.
voice.opening: Your number is on the line. Which end is it nearer?
voice.onFinish: You took the nearer one every time, and then asked whether to take it at all.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any number, any place, and the judgement bay open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: When rounding a number would be wrong

placement.where: After rounding has been done once on paper by rule. The tool is what puts the two candidates either side so the rule can be seen to be a description of nearness rather than a trick.

answer_key.rule: To round to a place, find the two nearest multiples of that place and take the nearer one. The rule reads the whole number to the right of the rounding place: five or more for tens, fifty or more for hundreds, five hundred or more for thousands, and then the digit at the rounding place goes up. Everything to the right becomes zero. Whether a number should be rounded depends on what it is for.
answer_key.wrong: The line zooms out and back in again with both candidates labelled and the halfway point marked, so the distance can be compared before the rule is read. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Eight is five or more, so the tens digit goes up from six to seven.
The ones place becomes zero, which gives 32,770.
items.question: Round 32,768 to the nearest ten.
items.checkpoint: The ones digit alone decides rounding to the nearest ten.
items.misconception: Rounding down to 32,760 by reading the tens digit instead of the ones.

steps: Cover the hundreds digit and read what is to its right. That is sixty-eight.
Sixty-eight is fifty or more, so the hundreds digit goes up from seven to eight.
The tens and ones both become zero, which gives 32,800.
items.question: Round 32,768 to the nearest hundred.
items.checkpoint: For hundreds you read the two digits to the right as a single number.
items.misconception: Looking only at the tens digit six and rounding down to 32,700.

steps: Cover the thousands digit and read what is to its right. That is two hundred eleven.
Two hundred eleven is less than five hundred, so the thousands digit stays at three.
The hundreds, tens and ones all become zero, which gives 43,000.
items.question: Round 43,211 to the nearest thousand.
items.checkpoint: For thousands you read the three digits to the right as a single number.
items.misconception: Rounding up to 44,000 because the hundreds place is not empty.

steps: Ask what the number is being used for.
A rounded crowd size is still useful, because nobody has to act on the exact figure.
A rounded starting time is not, because somebody has to arrive at it.
items.answer: No, because somebody has to act on it and a rounded start makes you late
items.question: A school begins at half past eight. Should that be rounded to the nearest ten minutes?
items.checkpoint: Rounding suits a number you only have to grasp, not one you have to act on.
items.misconception: Applying the rounding rule because a number is there, without asking what it is for.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Round 32,529 to the nearest hundred.
items.final_answer: 32,500. The two digits to the right are twenty-nine, which is under fifty

items.question: Round 7552 to the nearest thousand.
items.final_answer: 8000. The three digits to the right are five hundred fifty-two, which is over five hundred

items.question: The human body has 206 bones. Should that be rounded to the nearest hundred?
items.final_answer: No. It is an exact count, and saying two hundred would state something untrue

items.question: There were 1875 people in an auditorium. Can that be rounded to the nearest thousand?
items.final_answer: Yes, to 2000. A crowd size is used to get a sense of how many, not to count heads

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: chooses rounding to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand
brings the two candidate multiples to the ends of the line
shows the midpoint between the two candidates
draws how far the number is from each candidate
moves the marker to the nearer candidate and writes the answer
highlights the digits that were read to make the decision
rounds one number three ways and lines the answers up
opens the judgement bay with a real quantity to argue about

teaching_notes: Draw the line every time for the first few numbers, and ask which end is nearer before anybody reads a digit. Rounding is choosing the nearer of two marks, and the rule is only a quick way of saying that; a child taught the rule first has a procedure with nothing under it. For the nearest hundred, make them cover the hundreds digit and read what is left out loud, because reading two digits as one number is the exact place this goes wrong. Round one number all three ways and line the answers up. Three different answers from one number surprises them, and it should. The judgement bay is the best question on the page and it has no single right answer.
generation_prompt: Build a rounding tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A horizontal number line carries a marker at the number being rounded. A place picker for nearest ten, hundred and thousand zooms the line so that exactly the two candidate multiples sit at its ends, with the halfway point marked between them and the marker's distance to each end drawn as a bar. A snap control animates the marker to the nearer candidate and writes the rounded answer. A rule strip beneath highlights the entire number to the right of the rounding place, not a single digit, and states the threshold being applied. A stack all three control rounds one number three ways and lines the answers up for comparison. A separate judgement bay presents a real quantity and asks whether it should be rounded at all, accepting a reason rather than scoring an answer. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Pick the place you are rounding to and let the line zoom. Look at which end your number is nearer to, then check the rule strip. Round the same number three ways and compare. Then decide whether a number should be rounded at all.
